title: The curve
hook: automaticity grows quickly at first and then levels off (Lally et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday, start tiny: a habit so small it's nearly impossible to skip. Did your thirty seconds happen, and did it stay thirty seconds or grow? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

How long does it take to form a habit? Ask around and sometimes a confident number comes back, said as if it were printed on the side of the brain. A week. A month. Some round figure from a poster. It's a reasonable question, and it turns out to have a more interesting answer than a number. A team of researchers in London decided to watch habits form in real life, day by day, and draw what they saw. What came out wasn't a deadline. It was a shape. Today's word is that shape.
screen: `HOW LONG DOES IT TAKE?` → `A NUMBER FROM A POSTER.` → `NOT A DEADLINE. A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: First, the experiment. Psychologist Phillippa Lally and her colleagues asked volunteers to pick one new behavior, something to eat, drink or do, and to do it once a day in the same setting, like a glass of water after breakfast or a walk before dinner. Each day, the volunteers rated how automatic it felt: how much it happened without thinking. Second, steep at first. When the researchers plotted those ratings, the early days showed the biggest gains. Each repetition in the beginning added a lot of automaticity. Third, then it levels off. Later repetitions added less and less, until the line flattened out near its peak. Not a staircase, not a straight ramp. A curve that rises fast and then settles into a plateau. Fourth, different curves for different people. The time it took to get close to that plateau varied widely from person to person and from behavior to behavior. Some habits settled fairly quickly. Others were still climbing when the study ended. So the honest answer to how long a habit takes is: it depends, and the curve matters more than the count. This changes how a practice can feel from the inside. In the early stretch, every day adds a lot, which can make it feel like hard work. Later, the same practice asks for less, and it can stop feeling like progress at all, because there's not much left to gain. That flat stretch isn't failure. It's the top of the curve: the place where something that once took effort now simply happens.
screen: `ONE NEW BEHAVIOR, ONCE A DAY.` · `STEEP AT FIRST.` · `THEN IT LEVELS OFF.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT CURVES, DIFFERENT PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what's become easy. Sit, and settle on the breath. Then think back over this path. Is there something that once took effort and now happens almost on its own? Opening the app. Finding the breath. Sitting still for the length of the bell. Pick one and hold it in mind for a moment. That's a curve that has already climbed. You don't have to feel proud or anything else about it. Just notice it, and let the breath carry on by itself. The bell holds the time.
The curve. Habits grow quickly at first and then level off, at a different pace for different people. Today's word.
Your line: the curve. Today, notice one thing that used to take effort and now just happens, and see it as the top of a curve, not the end of progress. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: People building a habit sometimes track how automatic it feels over the weeks rather than counting toward a fixed number of days, expecting fast early gains that then level off.

trapdoor: what you thought: a habit forms after a fixed number of days.
what it means: automaticity grows fast at first, then levels off, at a different pace for each person.
what a scholar hears: Lally's team fit an asymptotic curve to daily self-ratings of automaticity, and the time to near the plateau varied widely across people and behaviors.

sources.ref: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts and Wardle, "How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world" (European Journal of Social Psychology)

notes: The index hook carries a year (2009); dropped under the claims rule. The study's median and range of days are deliberately not stated.

Confirm: volunteers chose an eating, drinking or activity behavior done once daily in the same context and self-rated automaticity daily; automaticity followed an asymptotic curve; time to reach near-plateau varied widely; some participants had not plateaued by the end of the study.
'A team of researchers in London' (University College London): confirm.
The study's finding about missed days is held for tomorrow (The curve forgives) and not taught here.
Editor pass: cut the stock phrase 'heavy lifting' (also used day 1283); the practice no longer calls breathing a habit with a curve, which the study doesn't support.
